F1.quote: IPTC Photo Metadata sets the industry standard for administrative, descriptive, and copyright information about images.
F1.claim: the standard defined by its operator's landing page: the industry standard for administrative, descriptive and copyright information about images
F1.lineage: the standard: what it is (the carrier the tests test)

F2.locus: Photo Metadata page: 'Critical to Photo and Related Businesses'
F2.quote: Photo metadata is key to protecting images' copyright and licensing information online. It is also essential for managing digital assets.
F2.claim: what photo metadata is for: protecting copyright and licensing information online; managing digital assets

F3.quote: IPTC not only defines the standard for photo metadata, but also conducts research about how it is used in the real world. We examine metadata in commonly used software, social media platforms, and more. The removal of rights information as images are transferred is of particular concern.
F3.claim: the tests named on the composition's own first card: research on how photo metadata is used in software and on social media platforms, the removal of rights information in transfer of particular concern
F3.lineage: the tests: what they are and what they check

F4.quote: The IPTC Photo Metadata Standard is the most widely used standard to describe photos, because of its universal acceptance among news agencies, photographers, photo agencies, libraries, museums, and other related industries.
F4.claim: the standard's self-description: the most widely used standard to describe photos, by its acceptance among news agencies, photographers, agencies, libraries and museums

F5.quote: Today, the IPTC Photo Metadata Standard consists of two schemas – IPTC Core and IPTC Extension – which were built on the legacy of the original IPTC-IIM, and developed by the IPTC for professional use with a focus on news and stock photos.
F5.claim: two schemas, IPTC Core and IPTC Extension, built on the legacy IIM, for professional news and stock photography
F5.lineage: the standard: what it is (the carrier the tests test)

F6.quote: IPTC worked alongside Adobe on the technical implementation of the metadata that employs Adobe’s XMP technology (now an ISO Standard) as an enriched alternative to the IIM format.
F6.claim: the implementation with Adobe in XMP (an ISO standard), an enriched alternative to IIM
F6.lineage: the standard's genealogy: IIM, IPTC headers, XMP

F7.quote: The 2025.1 version, published in November 2025, adds four new properties to handle metadata for AI-generated content: AI Prompt Information, AI Prompt Writer Name, AI System Used and AI System Version Used.
F7.claim: 2025.1 (November 2025) adds four properties for AI-generated content

F8.locus: 'What’s Defined by This Standard', last paragraph
F8.quote: How Photo Metadata formats are stored within image files are defined by non-IPTC file format standards, such as JPEG/JFIF, TIFF, PNG and more.
F8.claim: the stated limit of scope: how the formats are stored inside image files is defined by non-IPTC file-format standards (JPEG/JFIF, TIFF, PNG)
F8.lineage: the standard's scope and limits: file formats, no technical metadata

F9.quote: This is the IPTC Photo Metadadata Standard 2025.1, including … IPTC Core Metadata Schema 1.5 … IPTC Extension Metadata Schema 1.9
F9.claim: the current release: 2025.1, with Core 1.5 and Extension 1.9 (the source's spelling 'Metadadata' kept)

F10.quote: IPTC Photo Metadata provides data about photographs and the values can be processed by software. Each individual metadata entity is called a property and they are grouped into Administrative, Descriptive and Rights-related properties.
F10.claim: the specification's definition: data about photographs processable by software, properties grouped as administrative, descriptive and rights-related
F10.lineage: the standard: what it is (the carrier the tests test)

F11.quote: Because the IPTC acknowledges these technical metadata standards of other bodies and does not wish to duplicate existing metadata properties, the IPTC Photo Metadata specification does not include any technical metadata.
F11.claim: the stated limit: no technical (camera) metadata; that is left to the camera manufacturers' standards
F11.lineage: the standard's scope and limits: file formats, no technical metadata

F12.locus: table of contents, Extension heading (and the section heading at the same place in the body)
F12.claim: the specification heads its Extension section '1.8' while 'About the Standard' and §4 give Extension 1.9 (marked internally_inconsistent: both loci cited)

loci: B3 'About the Standard': 'IPTC Extension Metadata Schema 1.9'
B3 table of contents and section heading: 'IPTC Extension schema 1.8 specifications'

F13.quote: Data mining prohibition or permission, optionally with constraints.
F13.claim: the Data Mining property: prohibition or permission of data mining, optionally constrained

F14.locus: Introduction, 'How IPTC Photo Metadata Evolved Over Time'
F14.quote: IPTC Core fields can be embedded in the IIM format and/or in the XMP format. A key challenge for metadata embedded in parallel in IIM and XMP is that the values are synchronised - this should be taken care of by the image management software.
F14.claim: Core fields embedded in IIM and/or XMP; values embedded in parallel must be synchronised by the image software
F14.lineage: the standard's genealogy: IIM, IPTC headers, XMP

F15.locus: 'IPTC is often asked which fields should be filled out as a minimum'
F15.quote: By defining this set of minimal metadata properties IPTC does not support any removal of existing metadata outside this set without the explicit permission of the copyright owner of the image. (In simple words: this is not a permission to strip off metadata and is not legal advice.)
F15.claim: the minimum set is no permission to strip other metadata
F15.lineage: the norm the tests measure against: embedded metadata must not be removed

F16.locus: 'Fundamental Guidelines for the Preservation of Embedded Metadata', principle 4
F16.quote: Copyright management information metadata must never be removed from the files. … Removal of such metadata impacts on the ability to assert ownership rights and is therefore forbidden by law in many countries.
F16.claim: the Embedded Metadata Manifesto, endorsed by the IPTC: copyright management information must never be removed; removal is forbidden by law in many countries
F16.lineage: the norm the tests measure against: embedded metadata must not be removed

F17.quote: Google displays three IPTC photo metadata fields, wherever available, for an image shown as search result. This tells the viewer who is the creator and who is the copyright holder of the image and what credit line should be shown next to the image.
F17.claim: Google Images displays three embedded fields: creator, copyright notice, credit line
F17.lineage: who reads the embedded fields: Google Images and the IPTC's tools

F18.locus: 'For developers and site administrators: how to ensure the fields are preserved in images on your site'
F18.quote: Your site’s digital asset management system, content management system, image management system or content delivery network may be stripping out embedded metadata fields. Some systems do this with the best of intentions, thinking that it will save a few bytes of bandwidth, but stripping out metadata actually infringes on the copyright holders' rights and may even be illegal in some countries.
F18.claim: site systems (DAM, CMS, image management, CDN) may strip embedded fields; stripping infringes rights and may be illegal
F18.lineage: stripping in transit: where the carrier is lost

F19.quote: It may be important to distinguish AI-generated images from "regular" images: for example, to avoid re-training AI models on content that was already generated by a model, to understand which images can fall under copyright and which cannot (in some jurisdictions) and to avoid misinterpreting generated images as being real photos.
F19.claim: why AI-generated images are marked: against re-training on generated content, for copyright, against mistaking them for photos
F19.lineage: marking AI-generated images, and the C2PA metadata invalidated

F20.locus: 'Applying Metadata to AI-generated Images', field suggestions
F20.quote: Creator is bound to the owner of the intellectual property of an image in many countries and there are first legal decisions that AI generated images are not considered as creative work generating an intellectual property. Therefore, our recommendation is to leave the Image Creator field empty.
F20.claim: for AI-generated images, leave Image Creator empty
F20.lineage: marking AI-generated images, and the C2PA metadata invalidated

F21.locus: 'Applying Metadata to AI-generated Images', field suggestions
F21.quote: The Digital Source Type field should be set to the URI value http://cv.iptc.org/newscodes/digitalsourcetype/trainedAlgorithmicMedia or http://cv.iptc.org/newscodes/digitalsourcetype/compositeSynthetic.
F21.claim: Digital Source Type set to trainedAlgorithmicMedia or compositeSynthetic
F21.lineage: marking AI-generated images, and the C2PA metadata invalidated

F22.quote: The IPTC Photo Metadata Working Group has released version 2025.1 of the IPTC Photo Metadata Standard, including properties that can be used for AI-generated content.
F22.claim: the Working Group releases 2025.1 with properties for AI-generated content

F23.quote: AI System Used … Definition: The AI engine and/or the model name used to generate this image.
F23.claim: AI System Used defined: the AI engine or model name used to generate the image

F24.locus: announcement, caption of the example image
F24.quote: This image contains the new IPTC Photo Metadata fields “AI Prompt Information”, “AI System Used” and “AI Prompt Writer Name”. Note that adding the new IPTC Photo Metadata properties has rendered the C2PA metadata invalid.
F24.claim: the stated limit: writing the new properties into the example image rendered its C2PA metadata invalid
F24.lineage: marking AI-generated images, and the C2PA metadata invalidated

F25.quote: The Information Interchange Model (IIM) is a file structure and set of metadata attributes that can be applied to text, images and other media types. It was developed in the early 1990s by the International Press Telecommunications Council (IPTC) to expedite the international exchange of news among newspapers and news agencies.
F25.claim: IIM: a file structure and metadata attributes, developed by the IPTC in the early 1990s for news exchange
F25.lineage: the standard's genealogy: IIM, IPTC headers, XMP

F26.quote: IIM metadata embedded in images are often referred to as "IPTC headers", and can be easily encoded and decoded by most popular photo editing software.
F26.claim: embedded IIM metadata: the 'IPTC headers', read and written by most photo software
F26.lineage: the standard's genealogy: IIM, IPTC headers, XMP

F27.quote: The Extensible Metadata Platform (XMP) has largely superseded IIM's file structure, but the IIM image attributes are defined in the IPTC Core schema for XMP and most image manipulation programs keep the XMP and non-XMP IPTC attributes synchronized.
F27.claim: XMP has largely superseded IIM's structure; IIM's attributes live on in IPTC Core for XMP
F27.lineage: the standard's genealogy: IIM, IPTC headers, XMP

F28.quote: Because of its nearly universal acceptance among photographers — even amateurs — this is by far IPTC's most widely used standard.
F28.claim: the encyclopedia's reading: by far the IPTC's most widely used standard, by nearly universal acceptance among photographers

F29.quote: Quick Guide to IPTC Photo Metadata and Google Images … explains how to check and update IPTC Photo Metadata for best results in Google Images search results, as introduced by Google in September 2018.
F29.claim: the Google Images display, introduced by Google in September 2018, and the IPTC's quick guide to it
F29.lineage: who reads the embedded fields: Google Images and the IPTC's tools

F30.quote: IPTC refers to metadata standards developed for the professional exchange and description of media. Unlike EXIF, which is heavily focused on technical capture information, IPTC metadata is commonly used to describe, organize and manage images.
F30.claim: a third party's account: IPTC metadata describes, organizes and manages images, against Exif's technical capture data
F30.lineage: the standard's scope and limits: file formats, no technical metadata

F31.quote: Metadata shouldn't be treated as an infallible form of copyright protection because it can be removed or modified, but it provides useful information that can travel with the image.
F31.claim: the stated limit: metadata can be removed or modified, so it is no infallible copyright protection
F31.lineage: stripping in transit: where the carrier is lost

F32.quote: IPTC maintains the technical standard that image creators can use to put their creator and copyright details inside image files. We call this “photo metadata”. Google extracts this information from photos in search results and displays it to help you find who owns the image.
F32.claim: the IPTC maintains the standard for creator and copyright details inside files; Google extracts and displays them
F32.lineage: who reads the embedded fields: Google Images and the IPTC's tools

F33.quote: In that case, the metadata might be stripped from your images by some software on your site. Sometimes this could be your Digital Asset Management system (such as Bynder, WebDAM or Extensis Portfolio). In other cases your Content Management System (such as WordPress or Drupal) might strip off metadata. Or it could be a Content Delivery Network that you use, such as Cloudflare or Cloudinary.
F33.claim: metadata that does not show may have been stripped by a site's DAM, CMS or CDN
F33.lineage: stripping in transit: where the carrier is lost

F34.quote: IPTC's Photo Metadata Inspector tool lets you see embedded metadata in many image files. For eligible images, a context menu will appear when you right-click on the image. Select "View IPTC Photo Metadata" and you will be taken to IPTC's Get Photo Metadata (GetPMD) tool which will display all metadata embedded in the image file.
F34.claim: the IPTC's browser extension passes a web image to GetPMD, which displays its embedded metadata
F34.lineage: who reads the embedded fields: Google Images and the IPTC's tools

F35.locus: card title (video; the watch page answered HTTP 429; title confirmed by YouTube oEmbed, channel IPTC)
F35.quote: Introduction and welcome, 20 years of IPTC Photo Metadata, Recent work
F35.claim: the IPTC's video: twenty years of IPTC Photo Metadata (title only)
F35.lineage: the operator: the IPTC and its Photo Metadata Working Group
F35.checked_against: the card's title in the registry's cite_list (oEmbed title agrees)

F36.quote: IPTC promotes the proper use of IPTC Photo Metadata and claims “embedded metadata should not be removed” from images shared on a photo platform or a system for sharing files or messages with images.
F36.claim: the claim the tests check: embedded metadata should not be removed from images shared on photo platforms or file and message systems
F36.lineage: the tests: what they are and what they check

F37.quote: To check which systems support this claim, IPTC checks about a dozen sites regularly: in 2013, in 2016 and now again in Spring 2019.
F37.claim: the tests defined: about a dozen sites checked regularly, 2013, 2016, Spring 2019
F37.lineage: the tests: what they are and what they check

F38.quote: Uploading an image with values in many fields of the IPTC Photo Metadata Standard , e.g. the latest Reference Image File . This implies that all embedded metadata values are known and can be checked.
F38.claim: the method: upload an image whose embedded values are all known
F38.lineage: the tests: what they are and what they check

F39.quote: Check if the image can be saved to a local device by a Save As function of the web browser. … Check if the image can be downloaded by a function of the tested system (e.g. a menu item). … are the embedded Exif and IPTC metadata (in the formats IIM and XMP) of the uploaded image still embedded?
F39.claim: the transformations: Save As and download; the test: are the embedded Exif and IPTC (IIM and XMP) still embedded
F39.lineage: the tests: what they are and what they check

F40.quote: If displayed: are these 4 relevant fields shown, correctly: Caption/description, Creator, Copyright Notice, Credit Line (= the 4Cs )
F40.claim: the four fields checked for display: caption, creator, copyright notice, credit line
F40.lineage: what the tests track: the 4Cs in the file

F41.locus: results, image-sharing sites: Pexels, pixabay, Unsplash
F41.quote: Pexels … Metadata is stripped off in SavedAs or downloaded files. … pixabay … Metadata is stripped off in SavedAs or downloaded files. … Unsplash … No embedded metadata displayed, metadata is stripped off in SavedAs or downloaded files.
F41.claim: Pexels, pixabay and Unsplash strip embedded metadata from saved and downloaded files

F42.quote: (Free account tested.) Some embedded metadata displayed. Embedded Creator replaced by account owner. SavedAs files have no XMP metadata.
F42.claim: Flickr replaces the embedded creator with the account owner; saved files lose XMP

F43.locus: results, file and message systems: Facebook, Twitter
F43.quote: No embedded metadata displayed. SavedAs files have no XMP metadata. A few rights related fields were retained in IIM and Exif. 2 IIM fields contain data generated by Facebook. … Twitter … No embedded metadata displayed. Metadata is stripped off in SavedAs files.
F43.claim: Facebook keeps a few rights fields in IIM and Exif and writes two IIM fields of its own; Twitter strips saved files

F44.locus: results, file and message systems: Dropbox, Microsoft OneDrive
F44.quote: Passed through original file, preview can be SavedAs with stripped off metadata.
F44.claim: Dropbox and OneDrive pass the original through; their previews save with metadata stripped

F45.quote: Download is not a main feature, SaveAs files keep the embedded metadata.
F45.claim: Behance's saved files keep the embedded metadata

F46.quote: IPTC not only defines the standard for photo metadata, but also conducts research about how photo metadata is used and implemented. Our most recent tests and studies:
F46.claim: the research as the IPTC's activity beside the standard
F46.lineage: the tests: what they are and what they check

F47.quote: IPTC was approached by users who discovered that when they shared photos via social media sites or systems, their embedded metadata disappeared.
F47.claim: the origin: users found their embedded metadata disappeared when shared
F47.lineage: the tests: origin, cadence and count

F48.quote: The IPTC Photo Metadata Working Group tested 15 social media sites in 2016 and 2013 to understand how image sharing, through upload and download, affects the integrity of embedded metadata as defined by IPTC standards and the Exif standard.
F48.claim: the Working Group tested 15 sites in 2013 and 2016 for how upload and download affect embedded metadata's integrity
F48.lineage: the tests: origin, cadence and count

F49.quote: Some social media sites or systems remove embedded information like copyright notes, the name of the creator, the description and more, while others protect photographers’ data better. The results show that it is not impossible to preserve metadata in a workflow.
F49.claim: the finding: some sites remove the embedded information, others protect it; preservation in a workflow is not impossible
F49.lineage: the tests' findings and the software study

F50.quote: The results, published in August 2014, look promising: … Half of the programs offered fields for photographers to enter rights information, including the date, the image’s creator, copyright notice, and rights usage term. … Two out of three programs helped users retrieve embedded rights data. … Unfortunately, two of the programs didn’t support rights metadata at all.
F50.claim: the software study (August 2014): half the programs offered rights fields, two of three retrieved them, two supported none
F50.lineage: the tests' findings and the software study

F51.quote: Wikipedia does not have an article with this exact name. … There were no results matching the query. The pages "IPTC photo metadata tests" and '"IPTC photo metadata tests"' do not exist.
F51.claim: Wikipedia has no article on the tests, and no article text with the phrase; the title IPTC_Photo_Metadata is also absent (raw HTTP 404)

F52.locus: article 'International Press Telecommunications Council', §IPTC Standards › Photo metadata ¶1
F52.quote: The IPTC defined a set of metadata properties that can be applied to images, part of a broader standard developed in the early 1990s and known as the IPTC Information Interchange Model (IIM). Embedded IIM image information is often referred to as an "IPTC header".
F52.claim: the operator's article: image metadata properties from the 1990s IIM, embedded as the 'IPTC header'
F52.lineage: the standard's genealogy: IIM, IPTC headers, XMP

F53.quote: The International Press Telecommunications Council (IPTC), based in London, United Kingdom, is a consortium of the world's major news agencies, other news providers and news industry vendors and acts as the global standards body of the news media.
F53.claim: the operator: a London consortium of news agencies and vendors, the standards body of the news media
F53.lineage: the operator: the IPTC and its Photo Metadata Working Group
